prs.title: fix: use "URI Too Long" as the error label for FST_ERR_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH
prs.body:
Refs #7231

The default response for `FST_ERR_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH` is a 414 but its body says `"error": "Bad Request"`. This changes it to `"URI Too Long"` so it matches the status code, the same way `FST_ERR_BAD_URL` pairs 400 with `"Bad Request"`.

The `frameworkErrors` docs still said only `FST_ERR_BAD_URL` and `FST_ERR_ASYNC_CONSTRAINT` are supported, but `FST_ERR_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH` has gone through `frameworkErrors` since #6716. I've added it to the list. I also added a short note that these router-level errors are handled before a route is matched, so `onRequest`/`onSend` hooks and `setErrorHandler` don't run for them, and that `frameworkErrors` is the place to add things like CORS headers.

Before / after, using the repro from the issue:

```
# main
414 onRequest skipped {"error":"Bad Request","code":"FST_ERR_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH",...,"statusCode":414}
# this branch
414 onRequest skipped {"error":"URI Too Long","code":"FST_ERR_MAX_PARAM_LENGTH",...,"statusCode":414}
```

I left the main part of the issue (running the full lifecycle for these errors) out of this PR on purpose. d66ebd12 deliberately made malformed and over-long URLs fail closed before any application not-found handler runs, and sending them through `onRequest` + `setErrorHandler` would undo part of that. If you'd rather go that way, or just log the request in the default path, I'm happy to follow up.

#### Checklist

- [x] run `npm run test` (lint, unit, types all pass)
- [x] tests and/or benchmarks are included
- [x] documentation is changed or added

prs.title: fix: do not quote the test glob in the TypeScript template
prs.body:
Fixes #756

The `test` script that `generate.js` writes for `fastify generate --lang=ts` (the CommonJS TypeScript template) wraps the glob in quotes:

```
c8 node --test -r ts-node/register "test/**/*.ts"
```

Because of the quotes the shell never expands the pattern, so `node --test` gets the literal string `test/**/*.ts`. Glob support in the test runner only landed in Node.js 21, so on Node.js 20 (still in the CI matrix) and older the runner looks for a file with that exact name and fails with `Could not find '.../test/**/*.ts'`, which is what the issue reports. On 22+ it happens to work because Node expands the pattern itself.

The JavaScript templates and the ESM TypeScript template already pass the glob unquoted (`test/**/*.test.js`, `test/**/*.ts`), so this just drops the quotes in `typescriptTemplate.scripts.test` to match them. With the shell expanding the pattern, the script works the same way on every Node version. A side effect is that `test/helper.ts` is no longer handed to the runner as a test file on Node 22+ (it showed up as an extra "test" before).

`test/generate-typescript.test.js` now expects the unquoted script and also asserts that the glob is not quoted.

How I verified:

`node --test test/generate-typescript.test.js` fails without the change to `generate.js` (strictEqual on the script) and passes with it. Full `npm test` passes (lint, template suites, 231 pass / 1 skipped in the CLI suite, tstyche).

Generated a project with the CLI and checked what `node` actually receives from the script's shell:

```
--- argv node receives, before (quoted):
[ 'test/**/*.ts' ]
--- after (unquoted):
[
  'test/plugins/support.test.ts',
  'test/routes/example.test.ts',
  'test/routes/root.test.ts'
]
--- npm test in the generated project (Node 26), after:
✔ support works standalone
✔ example is loaded
✔ default root route
ℹ tests 3
ℹ pass 3
ℹ fail 0
```

Before the change the same project on Node 26 reported `tests 4` because `test/helper.ts` was also run as a test file. I did not have a Node 20 binary available locally, so the literal-pattern failure on 20 is based on the argv shown above plus the Node changelog (glob support for `node --test` added in v21), not a run on 20.

Left out on purpose:

- With `sh`, `**` behaves like `*`, so the expanded pattern only matches one directory level (`test/*/*.ts`). That is the same as the other templates today and covers the generated layout; I did not try to change that.
- Separately, the generated TS project currently fails `npm run build:ts` with TypeScript 6 (`TS5011`, `rootDir` must be set) and ts-node can't find Node types in tests. That's unrelated to this issue; for the run above I pinned `typescript@5` in the scratch project.

prs.title: fix: stop saveRequestFiles after a file hits the fileSize limit
prs.body:
Refs #470

I reproduced this on main with a real request: two 4 MB files, `limits: { fileSize: 1000 }`, the default `throwFileSizeLimit`, sent in 64 KB chunks.

The temp files themselves were never leaked. When `saveRequestFiles()` throws, its catch block already runs `cleanRequestFiles()`, so the directory was empty both after the error and after a second `cleanRequestFiles()` call. The comments were right about the other half, though: the error only came back after the whole body had been read, and the second file was fully written to disk before that.

The cause is in `saveRequestFiles()` in `index.js`. Once busboy hits `fileSize`, it marks the file stream `truncated` and ends it normally, so `pump(part.file, target)` resolves and the loop moves on to the next part. The `RequestFileTooLargeError` set by the `limit` listener is only stored as `lastError`, and the iterator hands it back when busboy finishes the request. `toBuffer()` doesn't have this problem because it checks `file.truncated` itself and throws.

The fix does the same check in `saveRequestFiles()`. After each file is written, if `part.file.truncated` is set and `throwFileSizeLimit` is on (read from the call options, otherwise the plugin default), it throws `RequestFileTooLargeError` with `err.part` set. The existing catch block then removes the partial temp file. When `throwFileSizeLimit: false`, nothing changes and truncated files are still saved.

Before (main):

```
response: 413 {"code":"FST_REQ_FILE_TOO_LARGE"}
body size: 8388994 client had sent 8454144 bytes when error surfaced
tmp files right after error: [] (tmpUploads entries: 2)
tmp files after cleanRequestFiles: []
tmp files after response: []
```

After:

```
response: 413 {"code":"FST_REQ_FILE_TOO_LARGE"}
body size: 8388994 client had sent 4325376 bytes when error surfaced
tmp files right after error: [] (tmpUploads entries: 1)
tmp files after cleanRequestFiles: []
tmp files after response: []
```

`test/fix-470.test.js` adds two tests:
- An oversized file followed by a second file. It checks that the error is `RequestFileTooLargeError` for the right part, that only one temp file was created, that the tmpdir is empty, and that the response is a 413. It fails on main.
- The `throwFileSizeLimit: false` case, which still saves both truncated files.

`npm test` passes: lint, 124 unit tests at 100% coverage, and tstyche.

What I left out on purpose: busboy still reads the oversized part through to its boundary before the error surfaces. With a single 3.7 GB file, the client still uploads the whole file before getting the 413. Failing at the moment the limit fires would mean either destroying the file stream mid-part and leaving the rest of the request unread, or closing the connection as suggested in the thread. Both change how the request and connection end, so I think that decision belongs with the maintainers and isn't part of this PR. That's why this says Refs and not Fixes.

prs.title: fix: return injected payload when express handles the request
prs.body:
Fixes #54

`fastify.inject()` returns an empty payload for any request that goes through the express stack. That covers express routes and routers, and also plain Fastify routes once any `fastify.use()` middleware is registered. The status code and headers are correct, but the body is `''`.

Root cause: `runConnect` in `index.js` hands `req.raw`/`reply.raw` to express, and express's `app.handle` (`express/lib/application.js`) does `Object.setPrototypeOf(res, this.response)`. For an injected request, `reply.raw` is a light-my-request `Response`. Its prototype overrides `write`, `end`, `writeHead` and a few more methods to collect the payload. Once the prototype is swapped, those overrides are lost and the plain `http.ServerResponse` methods write to the mock socket instead. The existing tests that use inject only check status codes, so this never showed up.

What changed: when `req.raw.isLightMyRequest` is set (a documented light-my-request marker), `runConnect` copies the own methods of the req/res prototype onto the instance before calling express. Express still swaps the prototype, but the instance properties shadow it, so light-my-request's methods keep working. Express's own methods (`res.json`, `res.send`, `req.get`, ...) are not affected because light-my-request doesn't define them. Requests from a real server never get this flag, so the normal HTTP path doesn't change.

Tests: added `test/inject.test.js`. It covers an express app route with `res.json` and a status/header, a router with `res.send` and `res.end`, a POST body parsed by `express.json()`, and a Fastify route (JSON and stream) behind an express middleware. All 5 fail without the change to `index.js` and pass with it. `npm test` passes: lint, 78 unit tests with 100% coverage, and tstyche.

Repro script (fastify 5.12.8, light-my-request 6.8.0, express 5.3.0): express routes mounted with `fastify.use()`, then `fastify.inject()`:

Before:
```
/json 200 application/json; charset=utf-8 ""
/send 201 text/plain; charset=utf-8 ""
/end 200 undefined ""
/app 200 application/json; charset=utf-8 ""
/body 200 application/json; charset=utf-8 ""
/f 200 ""          <- fastify route behind fastify.use((req, res, next) => next())
```

After:
```
/json 200 application/json; charset=utf-8 "{\"hello\":\"world\"}"
/send 201 text/plain; charset=utf-8 "text body"
/end 200 undefined "raw end"
/app 200 application/json; charset=utf-8 "{\"from\":\"app\"}"
/body 200 application/json; charset=utf-8 "{\"a\":1}"
/f 200 "{\"fastify\":true}"
```

Left out: I only copy methods from the immediate prototype of the injected req/res. That prototype is the one light-my-request builds, and it also covers its custom `Request` option, because light-my-request copies its methods onto that constructor's prototype. Methods that a user-supplied `Request` class inherits from further up its own chain are not preserved. I didn't add a README note because inject should now just work.

prs.title: feat: add serializer option for session data
prs.body:
Fixes #278

Session data goes through a hardcoded `JSON.stringify` in `encodeSecureSession` and `JSON.parse` in `decodeSecureSession` (index.js). Putting a BigInt in the session makes `JSON.stringify` throw `TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt`, and the request ends in a 500. There was no way to change how the data is encoded.

I didn't change the default encoding. Turning BigInts into strings by default (as #307 tried) would mean they come back as strings, and that changes what's stored for everyone. Instead this adds an opt-in `serializer` option:

```js
fastify.register(require('@fastify/secure-session'), {
  key,
  serializer: {
    stringify: (data) => JSON.stringify(data, (_key, value) =>
      typeof value === 'bigint' ? { $bigint: value.toString() } : value),
    parse: (text) => JSON.parse(text, (_key, value) =>
      value !== null && typeof value === 'object' && typeof value.$bigint === 'string'
        ? BigInt(value.$bigint)
        : value)
  }
})
```

Changes:
- `index.js`: each session's options take `serializer` (default `JSON`). It's stored with the session's key and expiry and used by `encodeSecureSession` / `decodeSecureSession`. Registration fails with `serializer must have stringify and parse functions` if either function is missing. `parse` gets the decrypted message as a string.
- `types/index.d.ts`: new `SessionSerializer` interface and an optional `serializer` field on `SecureSessionPluginOptions`.
- `README.md`: a "Custom serializer" section with the BigInt example and two caveats: `__ts` has to round-trip as a number, and if you switch serializers, `parse` still has to read old cookies.
- `test/serializer.test.js`: tests a BigInt round trip through real requests (top-level and nested), checks that the encode/decode decorators call the serializer, checks per-session serializers with multiple sessions, and checks the validation error. Type tests are in `types/index.tst.ts`.

Verification. Repro script: a POST route sets `9007199254740993n`, and a GET route reads it back from the cookie.

Before (main) and after with no `serializer`, which is unchanged:
```
POST 500 Do not know how to serialize a BigInt
```

After, with the serializer above:
```
POST 200 set-cookie present: true
GET 200 {"type":"bigint","value":"9007199254740993"}
```

With index.js reverted, all 4 new tests fail. With types/index.d.ts reverted, the type tests fail. `npm test` passes: 54 unit tests with 100% coverage, 18 tstyche assertions. Lint is clean.

Left out on purpose: there's no built-in BigInt encoding, and I didn't catch errors thrown by a custom `parse`. Those errors propagate the same way a `JSON.parse` failure would today.

prs.title: docs: explain typing a custom decoratorName in TypeScript
prs.body:
Fixes #344

When the plugin is registered with `decoratorName: 'jwtUser'`, the decoded token is stored on `request.jwtUser`, but nothing in the types knows about that property, and the README did not say how to declare it. The snippet in the issue does two things that look reasonable but have no effect:

- it augments `FastifyRequest` inside `declare module '@fastify/jwt'`. `FastifyRequest` belongs to the `fastify` module (types/index.d.ts augments it there), so this declares an unrelated, unused interface.
- it adds a `jwtUser` key to `FastifyJWT`. `UserType` in types/index.d.ts only reads the `user` key, which is the name of the user type, not the decorator.

There is no typing bug in `types/index.d.ts`; the property name is a runtime option the types cannot follow, so the fix is documentation.

Changes:

- README, TypeScript section: new "Custom decorator name" subsection showing `FastifyRequest` augmented in `fastify`, and explaining that `user` in `FastifyJWT` keeps that name whatever `decoratorName` is (it still types `formatUser`'s return value). The `decoratorName` option section links to it.
- `types/decorator-name.tst.ts`: tstyche test for the documented setup (`request.jwtUser` typed, `jwtSign` payload type, `formatUser` input/return checked against `FastifyJWT`).

Verification

Issue snippet, as a tstyche test on main:

```
fail ./types/repro.tst.ts
Error: Property 'jwtUser' does not exist on type 'FastifyRequest<RouteGenericInterface, ...>'. ts(2339)
```

The README snippet extracted verbatim into a `.d.ts` + `.ts` pair and checked with `tsc --strict`, resolving `@fastify/jwt` to `types/index.d.ts`:

```
tsc exit 0
```

Same files with `declare module "fastify"` switched to `declare module "@fastify/jwt"` (the issue's variant):

```
readme-check/index.ts(12,11): error TS2339: Property 'jwtUser' does not exist on type 'FastifyRequest<...>'.
tsc exit (issue variant) 2
```

The new type test also fails (2 of 6 assertions) if its `fastify` augmentation is moved into `@fastify/jwt`. `npm test`: lint clean, 201/201 unit tests, 100% coverage, 3 type test files / 52 assertions passing.

Left out: `request.user` stays declared on `FastifyRequest` even when a custom `decoratorName` is used (it is just not set at runtime). Removing it would need the decorator name to flow into the types, which is a design change rather than a docs fix; the README notes the behaviour instead.

prs.title: feat: allow callbackUriParams to be a function of the request
prs.body:
Fixes #306

`callbackUriParams` is only accepted as a static object (`index.js`, the option check in `fastifyOauth2` and the `urlOptions` built in `generateAuthorizationUriCallbacked`). That makes it impossible to put per-request values such as `login_hint` into the authorization uri that `startRedirectPath` redirects to. The only per-request hook that exists is the internal `kGenerateCallbackUriParams` symbol used by the Apple configuration, which isn't public and can't be set when using `discovery`. The current workaround is to drop `startRedirectPath`, call `generateAuthorizationUri` in your own route and edit the returned URL by hand.

This follows what #258 did for `callbackUri`: `callbackUriParams` can now also be a `(request) => object` function. It is called each time an authorization uri is generated (both for `startRedirectPath` and `generateAuthorizationUri`), and its result goes through the provider-specific hook as before, so Apple still gets `response_mode=form_post`. Passing an object works exactly as before.

Changes:
- `index.js`: accept a function in the option check, resolve it with the request before building the url options.
- `types/index.d.ts`: `callbackUriParams?: Object | ((req: FastifyRequest) => Object)`.
- README: short example using `login_hint` from a cookie with discovery.
- Tests: function used via `startRedirectPath` (two requests, different hints), via `generateAuthorizationUri`, and together with the Apple provider hook; type test for the function form.

Verified with `npm test` (lint, unit with 100% coverage, tstyche). New tests run against the unchanged `index.js`:

```
✔ options.callbackUriParams should be an object
✔ options.callbackUriParams
✖ options.callbackUriParams as a function
✖ options.callbackUriParams as a function with generateAuthorizationUri
✖ options.callbackUriParams as a function keeps provider specific params
  Error: options.callbackUriParams should be a object
```

With the change:

```
✔ options.callbackUriParams should be an object
✔ options.callbackUriParams
✔ options.callbackUriParams as a function
✔ options.callbackUriParams as a function with generateAuthorizationUri
✔ options.callbackUriParams as a function keeps provider specific params
ℹ tests 109
ℹ pass 109
ℹ fail 0
```

Left out on purpose: async functions (kept sync like `callbackUri`), and a separate public `generateCallbackUriParams(params, request, scope, state)` option. The function form covers the use case in the issue; happy to add the other one if you'd prefer that shape. The validation error message changed from "should be a object" to "should be a object or a function".

prs.title: fix: detect TypeScript loaders preloaded with require()
prs.body:
Fixes #404

`lib/runtime.js` decides whether `.ts` files can be loaded. For `@swc/register`, `@swc-node/register`, `tsm` and `esbuild-register` it only checks `process._preload_modules` (`checkPreloadModules`). Node fills that list only for its own `-r`/`--require` flag. `fastify start -r @swc-node/register` preloads the module with a plain `require()`, so the loader is active but autoload doesn't see it and skips `.ts` files unless `FASTIFY_AUTOLOAD_TYPESCRIPT` is set.

As suggested in the issue, I added a fallback that checks `require.cache`:

- `checkPreloadModules` now falls back to `checkRequireCache`. On first use, `checkRequireCache` collects the package names of everything in `require.cache` into a `Set`, so the cache keys are scanned once per process. Each runtime getter is already cached, so in practice this runs once.
- The package name is taken from the innermost `node_modules` segment and handles both `/` and `\`. That means pnpm's `.pnpm/.../node_modules/@swc-node/register/...` layout and Windows paths work, and it does not depend on `process.cwd()`. That was one of the concerns raised on #406.
- The existing checks still run first and haven't changed. The only new fallback outside `checkPreloadModules` is on `tsx`, because `-r tsx/cjs` has the same problem.
- Matching is on exact package names, so `@swc/core`, `esbuild` or `tsm-utils` being loaded does not enable TypeScript support.

The code runs inside the CJS module itself, so `require.cache` is available even when the app is ESM. That was the other concern raised on #406.

How I verified it: the repro script below simulates the fastify-cli preload with `require()`. I ran it with `--no-experimental-strip-types` so that native type stripping on recent Node doesn't hide the result:

```js
const root = process.argv[2]
require(require.resolve('@swc-node/register', { paths: [root] }))
const runtime = require(root + '/lib/runtime')
console.log('_preload_modules:', JSON.stringify(process._preload_modules))
console.log('runtime.swc:', runtime.swc, 'supportTypeScript:', runtime.supportTypeScript)
```

Before:
```
_preload_modules: []
runtime.swc: false supportTypeScript: false
```

After:
```
_preload_modules: []
runtime.swc: true supportTypeScript: true
```

The new tests in `test/issues/404/test.js` cover these cases:

- a real `require('@swc-node/register')`
- cache entries for `@swc/register`, `tsm`, `esbuild-register` and `tsx`
- a pnpm layout
- a Windows path
- negative cases with similarly named packages

Each case runs in a child process because the runtime checks are cached per process. Coverage is turned off for those children so they don't skew the report. Without the change in `lib/runtime.js`, 5 of the 6 tests fail; the negative case passes either way. `npm test` passes, including lint, tstyche, the loader scripts, jest, vitest and borp, with coverage still at 100%.

Not included: no changes to fastify-cli, and no README change. The `FASTIFY_AUTOLOAD_TYPESCRIPT` override is still documented and still works.

prs.title: docs: show how to type separator properties as string[]
prs.body:
Fixes #157

The `separator` keyword (`index.js`, `separator.compile`) replaces the string value with `data.split(separator)` (or `[]` for an empty string), so the property ends up as `string[]` even though the schema says `type: 'string'`. The README never said how to type that.

The types don't need to change. `EnvSchemaOpt<T>['schema']` is `JSONSchemaType<T> | AnySchema`, so a plain schema object is accepted whatever `T` is, and `envSchema<{ ALLOWED_HOSTS: string[] }>(...)` returns `string[]` for that key. The error in the issue (`Type '"string"' is not assignable to type '"array"'`) comes from TypeScript 5.1 and older checking the inline literal against the `JSONSchemaType<T>` member of that union. From TypeScript 5.2 on, the issue's own snippet compiles unchanged against the current `types/index.d.ts`:

```
TS 4.9.5  current d.ts: a.ts(8,38): error TS2322: Type '"string"' is not assignable to type '"array"'.
TS 5.1.6  current d.ts: a.ts(8,38): error TS2322: Type '"string"' is not assignable to type '"array"'.
TS 5.2.2  current d.ts: (no errors)
TS 5.3.3  current d.ts: (no errors)
TS 5.9.3  current d.ts: (no errors)
TS 6.0.3  current d.ts: (no errors)
```

On 5.1 and older, declaring the schema as a separate `const` and passing it to `envSchema<Env>({ schema })` avoids the error.

## Changes

- README, TypeScript section: an example passing an interface with `ALLOWED_HOSTS: string[]` and a typebox example using `Type.Unsafe<string[]>({ type: 'string', separator: ',' })`. It also says what you get for an empty or unset value.
- `types/index.tst.ts`: type tests for both patterns, checking that `ALLOWED_HOSTS` is `string[]`.

## Verification

Runtime behaviour on the default branch, which the README note describes:

```
H='a,b'                              {"H":["a","b"]}
H='a'                                {"H":["a"]}
H='' (empty)                         {"H":[]}
H='a,,b,'                            {"H":["a","","b",""]}
H=' a , b '                          {"H":[" a "," b "]}
H missing, optional                  {}
H missing, required                  throws: env must have required property 'H'
H missing, default 'x,y'             {"H":["x","y"]}
H='' required                        {"H":[]}
```

So an unset optional variable with no default is left out of `config` entirely, not turned into `[]`. That is why the README says to make the property optional in that case.

The new type tests pass. If I change the expectation to `string`, both fail with `Type 'string[]' is not the same as type 'string'`, so they really check the array type.

`npm run lint` is clean and `npm test` passes: 48/48 unit tests with 100% coverage, and 23/23 tstyche assertions.

I also checked json-schema-to-ts 3.1.1 separately. `FromSchema` gives `string` for the property, and `FromSchema<typeof schema, { deserialize: [{ pattern: { type: 'string', separator: ',' }, output: string[] }] }>` gives `string[]`. I didn't add that to the README because it has no json-schema-to-ts section and the package isn't a dev dependency.

Left out on purpose: no changes to `types/index.d.ts`, and no attempt to make `JSONSchemaType<T>` itself accept `type: 'string'` for a `string[]` field. That would mean replacing ajv's type, which is a design decision.
